: JUDGMENT :

The petitioner has filed this petition under Section 34(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and requested this Court to set aside the common Arbitral Award dated 10.03.2020 passed in case No.LAQ/ARB/NH-04/CR/06/2010-11.
.2.
In the petition it is stated that National Highways Authority of India was constituted by an Act of the Parliament, "the National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988" .

entities.text: National Highways Authority of India Act, 1988
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It is responsible for the development, maintenance and management of National Highways entrusted to it and for matters connected or incidental thereto.

.3. It is stated that the Central Government for the purpose of widening of NH-4 on the stretch of land from kms.10 to kms. 29.50 of Bengaluru-Nelamangala Section issued preliminary Notification dated 22.11.2006 (1st Stage of acquisition) under Section 3-A(1) of the National Highways Act, 1956 in-respect of acquisition of lands situated at Chikkabidrakallu village, Dasanapura Hobli, Bengaluru North Taluka.

The final notification was published in the official Gazette on 13.11.2007.
.4.

It is stated that under the said notification for the 1st stage of acquisition, amongst other lands the Non-agricultural (NA) lands in Sy.No.46/1 to an extent of 206.8Sq. Mtrs. equivalent to 2,226 Sq.
ft., situated at the said Village belonging to the 1 st Respondent were also acquired.
It is stated that in accordance with Section 3(a) of the NH Act, the respondent No. 3 was appointed as the competent authority by the Central Government.
.5. It is stated that the respondent No.3 vide award dated 10.04.2008 determined the market value of NA lands at Rs.250/- per sq. ft.

In order to determine compensation, the 3rd respondent had procured from the office of the Sub-Registrar, Bangalore North Taluk, the Sales Statistics from 23.11.2005 to 22.11.2006 (preceding one year) and the Guidance Value for the relevant period for both agricultural and Non- agricultural (NA) lands in the said Village.

The respondent No. 3 after examining both village and after conducting spot inspection opined that the sale statistics was not in consonance with the prevailing market value and hence relied upon the guidance value and determined the market value of NA lands at Rs.250/- per Sq.ft.
Being dissatisfied with the amount awarded by Respondent No.3, the 1st Respondent approached the 2nd Respondent under Section 3-G(5) of the NH Act.
.6. It is stated that the petitioner entered appearance and filed its Statement of objections with documents as well as written submissions with several Judgments in support of its defence.
The 2 nd Respondent has enhanced the market value from Rs.250/- per Sq. ft to Rs.962/- per Sq. ft. by treating them as commercial lands abutting National Highway.
A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
2 .7. Being aggrieved by the impugned Arbitral Award, the petitioner has preferred this petition on the following grounds:

The impugned Arbitral Award passed by the respondent No.2 is perverse, patently illegal;
 The Respondent No. 2 has grossly erred in not following the provisions of NH Act i.e., Section 3G(7)(a), the substantive law while passing the impugned award which is contrary to the provisions of Section 28 of A & C and accordingly the impugned Arbitral award is patently illegal;

The 2nd Respondent has not complied with the provision of Section 28 of the A & C Act, while passing the impugned award and therefore it is patently illegal and requres to be set aside.
 The respondent No. 2 has not made any attempt to investigate the market value of the subject lands as on the date of publication of preliminary notification.

The Preliminary Notification in respect of Chikkabidrakallu village was published on 22nd November 2006 whereas, the Notification relied upon the 2nd Respondent came into effect from 19th April 2007 i.e., after a lapse of more than 5 months from the date of publication of Preliminary Notification.
Hence, the Respondent could not have relied upon the same for the purpose of enhancement compensation.

The respondent No.2 has held that as per the aforesaid Notification, the guidance value of agricultural lands situated at Chikkabidrakallu Village was Rs.1,50,00,000/- Acre,
NA lands was Rs.425/- per Sq. ft and that of Gramathana was Rs. 350/- per Sq.ft.
In order to re- determine the market value for agricultural lands, the 2nd respondent taken the rate of Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre equivalent to Rs.344/- per Sq.ft. as the basis.
Thereafter the 2nd Respondent has added 60% on the same and arrived at Rs.550/-.

Further the 2nd Respondent has concluded that since the acquired lands are abutting NH and commercial in nature, further percentage of 75 has to be added on Rs.550/- and arrived at Rs.962/- per Sq. ft. i.e. Rs.550/- + Rs.412/- (75% of Rs.
550/-).

It is relevant to mention here that the entry at page No.288 Sl. No.15 provides for guidance value of NA lands situated at Chikkabidrakallu Village as Rs.425/- per Sq. ft. but Sl.No.15 (a) does not provide for guidance value of NA lands abutting NH.
On one hand the 2nd Respondent has stated at page 7 of the Arbitral award that the guidance value of NA lands of Chikkabidrakallu village is Rs.425/- per Sq.ft.
But nowhere has relied upon the said rate in so far as NA land are concerned.
Consequently, the statement of the 2 nd Respondent that the enhancement is made on the basis of the Notification dated 17 April 2007 is completely false.

A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
3
There is absolutely no justification for the addition of 60% and 75% which renders the impugned Arbitral award completely illegal.
The Notification dated 17th April 2007 is a document which did not form a part of the Arbitral proceedings and the Petitioner was never given an opportunity to rebut the same.
Hence the impugned Arbitral award is contrary to provisions of Section 24 of the A and C Act.
There are manifest errors in the impugned Arbitral award and consequently the same is liable to be set aside under Section 34(2A).
The impugned Arbitral award is not a speaking order and liable to be set aside.

The 2nd respondent has neither complied with the procedure provided under Section 24,
nor decided the dispute in accordance with Section 28(1)(a) and at the same time has failed to comply with Section 31(3) of the A & C Act, thus rendering the impugned Arbitral award opposed to settled position of law.
The signed copy of the impugned Arbitral award was never served upon the Petitioner.

The 2nd respondent has violated the provision of Section 31(5) of the A & C Act.
.8.
The petitioner submits that the impugned Arbitral award was passed on 10th March 2020.
The copy of the impugned arbitral award was received for the first time by the Petitioner on 27th November 2020 through the 3rd Respondent.

Petition is being filed in accordance with the order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Suo Moto W.P. (Civil) 3/2020 excluding the period of limitation period between 15th March 2020 till 14th March 2021.
Hence, the petition is in time.

.9. The respondent No.1 has filed objections stating that application is being filed with malicious intention and ulterior motive and nothing but the petitioner is trying to make unlawful gain of the property owned by the respondent herein.
The impugned order which is under challenged has clearly stated as to and what circumstances the award amount has been enhanced from Rs.250per Sq.ft to Rs.962per sq.ft.
And hence the petitioner cannot find fault with the said calculations and hence the petition is misconceived.
The 2nd respondent has held that the guidelines value of the agricultural land situated at Chikka Biddarakallu village is Rs.1,50,00,000/- per acre and accordingly the N.A. lands is 425 per sq. ft.
And that of the gramathana is 350 per sq. ft.
And this aspect demonstrates that the 2nd respondent has done his home work prior to passing of the order which is under challenge in this matter.
Hence, prayed for dismissal of the petition.

.10. The following points that would arise for my consideration are:
(1) Whether petitioner in A.P. No.116/2021 has made out sufficient grounds under Section 34(2) of Arbitration and Conciliation Act to set aside the arbitral award dated 10.03.2020 passed by respondent No.2?
A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
4
(2) What order or award?

.11. My findings on the above points are:
Point No.1 : In the Negative Point No.2 : As per final order, for the following:
REASONS 12. POINT No.1: The respondent No. 3 has acquired non agricultural land in Sy.No.
46/1 to an extent of 206.8 sq. meters equivalent to 2226 sq. feet situated at Chikkabidarakallu village under the preliminary notification dated 22.11.2006.
The respondent No. 3 has determined the market value of NA lands at Rs.250/- per sq. ft.
The respondent No. 1 being dissatisfied with the award amount had approached the respondent No. 2 under Section 3-G(5) of NH Act.
The respondent No. 2 has re-determined the the market value at Rs. 962/- per sq. ft.
Being aggrieved by the said award, the petitioner has filed this petition under Section 34 of Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
13. It is necessary to bear in mind the scope of this Court to interfere with the award passed by the Arbitrator.
Section 34(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provide the circumstances under which an award can be set aside by a civil Court.

It provides that- 1) if a party was under some incapacity; or 2) that the arbitration agreement is not valid under any law which the parties are subjected to ; or 3) the party was not given proper notice of the appointment of the arbitrator or arbitral proceedings; or 4) that the award is not within the terms of the arbitration agreement; or 5) the composition of arbitral tribunal or the arbitral procedure is not accordance with the agreement of parties;
6) that the arbitral award is in conflict with the pubic policy of India etc.,

Explanation shows that an award is in conflict with the pubic policy of India (i) if the making of the award was induced or affected by fraud or corruption or was in violation of Section 75 or Section 81.
(ii) It is in conflict with contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian Law or (iii) It is in conflict with most basic notion of morality or justice.

A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
5 Explanation 2.
The test as to whether there is contravention with the fundamental policy of Indian law shall not entail a review on the merits of the dispute.

2A It may also be set aside if the Court finds the award is vitiated by patent illegality appearing on the face of award provided that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of law or by re appreciation of evidence.
Bearing in mind the above section, now it has to be seen whether the impugned award suffers from any patent error illegality as envisage in the above section.
.14. The petitioner has stated that the respondent No.3 Arbitrator has relied upon the notification dated 17.04.2007 which came into effect from 19.04.2007.
Preliminary notification in the present case was issued on 20.11.2006.

It is stated that as per Substantial Law NH Authority Act Section 3-G(7)(a), the arbitrator while determining the amount shall take into consideration the market value of the land as on the date of publication of the notification under Section 3-A of NH Act.

It is argued that the respondent No.2 could not have relied upon the guidelines value which came into effect after publication of preliminary notification dated 20.11.2006.
.15.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd., Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd. (AIR 2003 SC 2629) has held that:
 "if the award is contrary to the  Substantive provisions of law or the provisions of the Act or against the terms of the contract, it would be patently illegal, which could be interfered under Section 34".
.16.

entities.text: Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd., Vs. SAW Pipes Ltd. (AIR 2003 SC 2629)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If at all the Arbitrator relied on the notification dated 17.04.2007, the respondent No. 2 should have deescalated the value to the date of preliminary notification.

.17. As per Rule No.5 of the Karnataka Stamps Constitution of Central valuation committee for estimation, publication and revision of market value guidelines of property rules 2003 deals with estimation of market value guidelines.

As per the said guidance the central valuation committee shall as far as possible in the first week of October of every calendar year send instruction along with general policy guidelines to all the committees in the state of estimation of market value guidelines of properties for the next calendar year.
Such instructions may be sent to any sub committee at any time of the calendar year for the revision of the rates, if required.

.18. Rule 7 of the above Karnataka Stamp rules states that the Secretary of the Central Valuation Committee on receipt of statement from the Registrar of a district shall verify and place them before the committee which shall meet in the third week of January in the next calendar year.

Sub rule 3 states that on approval of the estimation of the each sub district/district, the statements shall be attested by the secretary on behalf of the committee who shall then send such approved statements of estimation of market value of properties to the Registrar of the districts in the 1st week of the March in the next calendar year and later shall forward it to the concerned sub committee within the A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
6 week of the receipt of the statements in such form as may be specified by the committee from time to time.
.19.

From the above rules it is clear that the process for fixing the guidelines value has commenced in the October 2006; that actually the market value of the property for the year 2006 which was published in 2007.

In circumstances reliance placed on the guidance value notification dated 17-04-2007 for reckoning the market value of the property acquired under preliminary notification dated 20-11-2006 by itself cannot be accepted to be a patent illegality committed by the 2nd respondent arbitrator.
20. The Arbitrator relying upon the guidelines value dated 17.04.2007 has redetermined the market value at Rs. 962/- per sq. feet.

The petitioner has stated that the guidance value of agricultural land situated at Chikkabidarakallu village was Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre, NA lands was Rs. 425/- per sq. feet and that of gramathana was Rs. 350/- per sq. feet.
In order to re
- determine the market value for NA lands

, the respondent No. 2 has taken the rate of agricultural land at Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre,
equivalent to Rs. 344/- per sq. feet.
He added 60% on the same and arrived at Rs.550/-.

Thereafter,
has held that the lands were abutting NH and that the lands acquired were commercial in nature on account of which the respondent No. 1 is entitled to addition of 75% on Rs. 550/- per sq. feet and arrived at Rs. 962/- per sq. feet.
provides that the guidance value of NA lands situated at Chikkabidarakallu village at Rs.425/- per sq.ft.
It does not provide for guidance value of NA lands abutting NH.

The special instruction to the A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
7 said notification provides that a percentage of 50 and 25 is to be added on the guidance for lands abutting NH and State Highway respectively when the guidance value of particular property is not specifically provided for under the notification.
The arbitrator had not relied upon the rate in so far as value of lands NA lands are concerned.
It would have been open for the arbitrator to take note of the value fixed for the commercial/gramatna sites.
It is stated that there is no justification for addition of 60% for NA, 75% on NH and commercial lands on Rs. 1,50,00,000/- per acre.
.23. In AIR 1987 SC 81 (M/s. Hindustan Tea Company v/s K. Sashikanth and another.

entities.text: AIR 1987 SC 81 (M/s. Hindustan Tea Company v/s K. Sashikanth and another
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that award cannot be set aside on the ground that Arbitrator reached wrong conclusion or he failed to appreciate facts.
.24. The finding of the Arbitrator is question of fact which cannot be taken up as cause for setting aside the Arbitral Award.
.25. The proviso to Sub Section (2A) of Section 34 of Act of 1996, clearly indicates that "An award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of erroneous application of law."

entities.text: proviso to Sub Section (2A) of Section 34
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text: In view of the above decision and the section 34(2) of the A and C Act the above contention of the petitioner cannot be examined.
.26. The Arbitrator has relied upon guidelines value dated 17.04.2007.
This document is not valid record received from the Arbitrator as none of the parties have produced and this is evident from the record of the Arbitrator.
Section 24(3) of the Act provides provision regarding hearing and written proceedings.

It reads thus:
"All statements, documents or other information supplied to, or applications made to the arbitral tribunal by one party shall be communicated to the other party, and any expert report or evidentiary document on which the arbitral tribunal may rely in making its decision shall be communicated to the parties".
.27.

As the Arbitrator has relied on the estimated guidelines value of immovable properties and buildings dated 17.04.2007 without bringing to the knowledge of the parties and thereby has failed to follow the procedure under Section 24 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
So the award has to be set aside on the ground of patent illegality.

.28. The petitioner has contended that the respondent No.2 has not assigned any reasons for re- determining the compensation nor he has assigned any reasons for enhancing the compensation or for relying upon notification dated 17.04.2007.
.29.

In Som Dutt Builders Ltd Vs. State of Kerala (2010)2 AWC (supp) 1390 SC) has held that:
"Reasons must be indicated in the award as that would reflect thought process leading to a particular conclusion.

entities.text: Som Dutt Builders Ltd Vs. State of Kerala (2010)2 AWC (supp) 1390 SC)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
To satisfy the requirement of Section 31(3), the reasons must be stated by the Arbitral Tribunal upon which the award is based; want A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
8 of reasons would make such award legally flawed."

.30. On perusal of the records and the award of the Arbitrator it is seen that the respondent No.2 has neither complied with the procedure provided under Section 24 nor decided the dispute in accordance with Section 28(1)(a) and at the same time has failed to comply with Section 31(3) of the A & C Act, thus rendering the impugned Arbitral Award opposed to settled position of law.

.31. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd. Vs. SAW Piles Ltd., (AIR 2003 SC 2629) has held that:
"if the award is patently against the statutory provisions of Substantive law which is in force in India or is passed without giving an opportunity of hearing to the parties as provided under Section 24 or without giving any reason in a case where parties have not agreed that no reasons are to be recorded, it would be against the statutory provisions.

entities.text: Oil & Natural Gas Corp. Ltd. Vs. SAW Piles Ltd., (AIR 2003 SC 2629)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In all such cases, the award is required to be set aside on the ground of 'patent illegality'
The above decision is applies to the case on hand.

.32. The respondent No.1 has stated that the Arbitrator has not taken into consideration additional market value of 12%, 30% solatium, 9% interest from the date of taking possession of the acquired land and 15% interest on additional market value and solatium.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court has in AIR 2019 SC 4689:
AIR Online 2019 SC 1087 - Union of India and another Vs. Tarsem Singh and others has held that:
"provisions of Land Acquisition Act relating to solatium and interest contained in S.23(1A) and (2) and interest payable in terms of Section 28 proviso - will apply to acquisitions made under National Highways Act - Consequently, S. 3-J to extent of granting compensation without solatium and interest - Is violative of Art. 14 of Constitution and, therefore, declared to be unconstitutional.

entities.text:
AIR 2019 SC 4689:
AIR Online 2019 SC 1087 - Union of India and another Vs. Tarsem Singh and others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: .33. In-spite of the decision of the the Hon'ble Supreme Court the respondent No.2 has ignored the direction of the Supreme Court and thus, he has not granted additional market value and solatium.
.34. Though the Arbitrator has not complied with Section 31(3) of the NH Act.
Endeavor of the Court should be honour and support the award as far as possible.
There is error committed by the Arbitrator in passing the award.

Since 12%
additional market value, 30% solatium and 9% on that interest for 1 year from taking possession and thereafter 15% till deposit has not been given, I feel if the same is given the compensation which respondent No. 1 would get more or less be the same as awarded by Arbitrator.

For the said reason I do not intend to interfere with the A.P./116/2021 on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/73195742/
9 award passed by the respondent No.2.
Hence, I answer point No.1 in the Negative .35.
Point No.2:

In view of the aforesaid finding on point No.1 I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER A.P. No.116/2021 is dismissed.
The impugned award passed by the respondent No.2 in so far as pertaining to case No.LAQ/ARB/NH-4/CR/06/2010-11 is confirmed.
